questions: Did the double vision begin suddenly?
Do you have double vision when both eyes are open?
Does the double vision disappear when either eye is covered?
Is the double vision worse when looking to one side or up/down?
Have you noticed drooping of either eyelid?
Is there pain around or behind either eye?
Have you noticed unequal pupil sizes?
Do you have weakness, numbness, difficulty speaking, severe headache, or imbalance?
Do you have diabetes, high blood pressure, or a history of stroke?
Have you recently had an eye injury or infection?
Does the eyelid drooping or double vision fluctuate during the day?
Is it worse late in the day or after prolonged reading or looking upward?
Does it improve after rest or sleep?
Do you have difficulty chewing, swallowing, speaking, or holding your head up?
Have you had episodes of shortness of breath or weakness in your arms or legs?
Does the drooping alternate between the two eyes?
Does either eyelid briefly lift after repeatedly squeezing your eyes shut?
orders: Bedside ocular motility examination in the nine cardinal positions of gaze, documenting each eye’s ability to abduct, adduct, elevate, and depress.
Bedside alternate cover test and prism measurement of ocular misalignment at distance and near.
Bedside examination of pupils in light and dark, including direct and consensual responses and a swinging-flashlight test.
Bedside fatigability test with sustained upgaze for 2 minutes and repeated forceful eyelid closure.
Ice-pack test applied to each ptotic upper eyelid for 2 minutes, with pre- and post-test measurement of palpebral fissure height.
Serum acetylcholine-receptor antibody panel, including binding, blocking, and modulating antibodies.
Repetitive nerve stimulation of the facial and proximal limb muscles.
Single-fiber electromyography of the orbicularis oculi.
MRI brain with diffusion-weighted imaging, focused on the brainstem and medial longitudinal fasciculi.
served: acetylcholine receptor, MuSK and LRP4 antibodies
